Have you ever wondered why BRICS is known as the “golden bricks” in China, even though there is no reference to gold in its English name?
According to an Eyes On report by Xinhua reporter Huang Aipung, the answer lies in the Chinese interpretation of the acronym and the economic significance associated with the grouping.
BRICS traces its origins to a 2001 research paper by Goldman Sachs economist Jim O’Neill, who grouped Brazil, Russia, India and China together as four rapidly growing emerging economies. Their initials formed “BRIC,” a name that sounds similar to the English word “brick.”
When the term entered Chinese usage, it received a distinctive translation. “BRIC” became “金砖” (jinzhuan), literally meaning “golden brick.” The expression added associations with value, growth and potential to the original acronym, according to the Xinhua report.
The four countries subsequently began meeting as a group, holding their first leaders’ summit in 2009. South Africa later joined, turning BRIC into BRICS.
The grouping has since expanded beyond its original members, welcoming countries including Egypt, Ethiopia and Indonesia. Its members now span Asia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America, giving the bloc a broader combined population, resource base, market reach and economic weight.
As Xinhua's Huang Aipung noted, the Chinese “golden bricks” translation appears increasingly fitting as the grouping has grown. Yet BRICS’ influence is not based solely on the size of its members. Cooperation has become an increasingly important part of its role.
BRICS countries have developed cooperation in areas including trade and finance, technology, healthcare and climate action. One of the group's key institutions is the New Development Bank, which has approved nearly $43 billion in financing for projects involving roads, railways, clean energy, water systems and digital infrastructure since its establishment.
The development illustrates how BRICS has evolved from an acronym created in a Goldman Sachs research paper into a platform for cooperation among emerging economies.
The grouping also seeks to strengthen the voice of the Global South in discussions over global development, with its expanding membership giving it greater collective reach.
The “golden brick” metaphor ultimately captures both the linguistic creativity behind the Chinese name and the growing weight of the BRICS grouping. One brick may have limited impact on its own, but many bricks brought together can form something much larger.
